title: As a developer, I can install dependencies from a lockfile and get the exact same resolved versions on every machine
As a platform-engineer, I can enforce a frozen/immutable lockfile mode that fails the install when the manifest and lockfile disagree
As a developer, I can pin exact versions of packages and tools per project and have the manager respect those pins
As a developer, I can bootstrap a fresh clone with one command that installs everything the project declares
As a developer, I can manage many packages in one monorepo with workspaces sharing a single lockfile and cross-linked local dependencies
As a developer, I can run installs and scripts filtered to a subset of workspace packages (including only those affected by a change)
As a developer, I can install and switch language runtimes or tool versions per project from a checked-in config file
As a developer, I can have the right tool versions and environment variables activate automatically when I enter a project directory
As a platform-engineer, I can audit installed dependencies for known vulnerabilities directly from the CLI
As a platform-engineer, I can turn on protections against malicious packages, such as blocking lifecycle scripts or enforcing a minimum release age
As a platform-engineer, I can trust that fetched packages are verified against checksums, signatures, or attestations before they run
As a developer, I can install prebuilt binary packages from a cache instead of compiling from source
As a developer, I can rely on a shared content-addressable store so the same dependency version is stored once on disk across all projects
As a platform-engineer, I can make CI installs fast with a documented cache-restore setup and offline-capable installs
As a developer, I can see published benchmarks or measured numbers backing the manager's speed claims
As a developer, I can use the same workflow and config on macOS, Linux, and Windows
As a switcher, I can migrate an existing project from the incumbent tool with documented import or conversion tooling
As a switcher, I can keep using familiar commands and interface conventions from the incumbent tool while adopting this manager
As a developer, I can install almost anything I need from a large, actively maintained package registry or repository
As a developer, I can extend the manager through third-party taps, overlays, plugins, or backends
As a platform-engineer, I can point the manager at private registries or mirrors with scoped authentication
As an AI-native user, I can get machine-readable (JSON) output from core commands so an agent can parse results instead of scraping text
As an AI-native user, I can have an agent install and update project dependencies non-interactively, with clear exit codes and errors when something fails
As an AI-native user, I can add, remove, and upgrade dependencies through CLI commands that safely rewrite the manifest and lockfile, so an agent never hand-edits them
As an AI-native user, I can point an agent at a documented, text-based lockfile format it can read and diff
